original_question: For the free Abelian groups Z^n with n > 3, compute the numbers χ(Z^n) and determine the structure of their central sets, where a central set E in a group G is one such that every r-coloring of G with r < ν(G) contains an infinite monochromatic subset symmetric with respect to some point x in E.
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem 2.4: calculate the numbers c(ℤ^n) and investigate the structure of central sets in ℤ^n for n>3.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the ambient objects (the free Abelian groups ℤ^n with n>3), the two tasks (compute the relevant numerical invariant and study the structure of central sets), and the intended Ramsey-theoretic notion of centrality via infinite monochromatic subsets symmetric about a point of the prescribed set.
missing_details: The paper’s invariant here is c(ℤ^n), not χ(ℤ^n); c(G) denotes the minimal cardinality of a central subset of G.
The definition of a central subset depends on the invariant ν(G), which in Section 1 is the least number of colors needed to color G so that there is no infinite monochromatic symmetric subset of G.
Because the target groups are Abelian and written additively, symmetry with respect to x should be made explicit as A=2x−A (equivalently, in multiplicative notation, A=xA^{-1}x).
The quantifier is over every finite r-coloring of G with r<ν(G), not over one fixed coloring or one fixed r.
To make “compute the numbers” stand alone, one must say that c(ℤ^n) is the minimum size of a central subset of ℤ^n.

The nearby context shows why the problem is posed only for n>3: Theorem 2.2 records exact values only in the already solved low-dimensional cases, and Theorem 2.3 explains those cases via minimal central subsets shaped as triangles and octahedra.

If one wants the structural part to match the paper’s discussion most closely, it helps to note that the solved cases analyze minimal central subsets, even though Problem 2.4 itself asks more broadly for the structure of central sets in ℤ^n.
refined_question: Let ν(G) be the least number of colors needed to color a group G so that G contains no infinite monochromatic subset symmetric with respect to any point, and call a subset E⊆G central if for every finite r-coloring of G with r<ν(G) there exists an infinite monochromatic subset A⊆G symmetric with respect to some x∈E (for G=ℤ^n, in additive notation, A=2x−A). For each n>3, determine c(ℤ^n), the minimum cardinality of a central subset of ℤ^n, and investigate the structure of central sets in ℤ^n.
justification: The draft is aiming at Section 2 rather than Section 1: Section 2 introduces central sets and minimal central sets, then poses two questions for an Abelian group G—describing the structure of central subsets of G and determining the minimal size of a central set in G. Theorem 2.1 reduces the latter size problem for infinite Abelian groups to the numbers c(ℤ^n); Theorem 2.2 states that exact values are known only in low dimensions; and Theorem 2.3 explains those solved cases through the geometry of minimal central subsets (triangles in ℤ^2 and octahedra in ℤ^3). The open problem that remains, and that your draft is clearly targeting, is therefore exactly Problem 2.4.
